summary: For ages 9–10: multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000 by understanding that each digit SHIFTS across the place-value columns — digits move left for multiplying and right for dividing, while the decimal point stays fixed. This replaces the fragile 'add a zero' rule, which breaks for decimals (3.45×100 is 345, not 3.4500), and the memorised 'move the point' rule, which gives the same numerical result but hides why the value changes and is easily misapplied (for example where to put the point in a whole number, or forgetting placeholder zeros). The skill underpins metric conversions and powers-of-ten notation.
misconceptions: 'Add a zero' rule misapplied to decimals (3.45×100 wrongly written as 3.4500).
'Move the decimal point' causing confusion about direction or number of places.
Shifting the wrong number of places for the power of ten.
Forgetting to fill empty places with zeros as placeholders when needed (e.g. 72÷1000 = 0.072).
Thinking dividing always makes the digits smaller in value without understanding the place shift.

activities.title: Sliding digits on a place-value chart
steps: Set up a place-value chart with labelled columns from hundreds down to thousandths (… H  T  O • t  h  th) and a fixed decimal point.
Place 3.45 in the columns, then multiply by 100: slide every digit TWO columns to the LEFT so the 3, 4 and 5 become 345. Note that nothing was appended — the digits moved.
Now test the tempting 'just add two zeros' shortcut on 3.45 and compare: it gives 3.4500, which is wrong. Discuss why the shortcut fails for decimals.
Divide 72 by 1000: slide every digit THREE columns to the RIGHT, and fill each empty column it crosses with a placeholder zero, giving 0.072 (including the leading 0).
Compute 6 × 10 by sliding one place left (giving 60), and connect the number of places shifted to the number of zeros in 10/100/1000 (×1000 → 3 places).
Optionally switch the chart to a metric mode so the same kind of shift is reread as a conversion: metres → centimetres is ×100 (two places left) and centimetres → millimetres is ×10 (one place left).
activities.insight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten changes what each digit is worth, so the digits shift the matching number of place-value columns; the decimal point does not move, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.

activities.title: Reference chart with reveal-able shift arrows
steps: Study a place-value chart annotated with arrows that show the shift for ×10 (one place), ×100 (two places) and ×1000 (three places), and the reverse for division.
Answer the prompt 'why isn't 3.45 × 100 = 3.4500?' and check your reasoning against a revealed explanation.
State in your own words how many places each power of ten shifts the digits and in which direction.
activities.insight: A clear reference links each power of ten to a fixed number of places and direction, reinforcing that the direction and count — not zero-appending — determine the result.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and fill-in consolidation
steps: Choose the correct value of 3.45 × 100 from options including the trap value 3.4500, and explain why the trap is wrong.
Find and fix the mistake in a worked example where a digit has been shifted the wrong number of places.
Explain, for one of your answers, how the value of each digit changed.
activities.insight: Consolidation surfaces the specific decimal trap (3.4500) and the placeholder-zero requirement (0.072), confirming whether digit-shift reasoning is secure rather than a fragile trick.

activities.title: Testing the 'just add a zero' claim out loud
steps: Respond to a character who insists you can always 'just add a zero' to multiply by ten.
Test the claim on a whole number (6 × 10 = 60) where it seems to work, then on a decimal (3.45 × 100) where it produces 3.4500.
Argue, using place value, why the claim is unsafe and what actually happens to the digits.
activities.insight: Articulating why 'add a zero' works for whole numbers but fails for decimals turns a half-learned rule into reasoned understanding of the digit shift.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to work these while you watch, using a place-value chart if they wish: 3.45 × 100, 72 ÷ 1000, and 6 × 10. Watch whether they SHIFT the digits across the place-value columns or whether they just 'add/remove zeros' or 'move the decimal point' as a rule.
checkAnswer: 345; 0.072; 60. The teacher watches for the child moving each digit the correct number of places (two places left for ×100, three places right for ÷1000) with the decimal point staying put and zeros filling empty places — not a memorised 'add two zeros' trick that breaks on decimals.
